'So when do you fly?' Varun asked, dropping onto the sofa beside her.
'Soon. The agent says the visa office changed the date again.'
'Again? That's the third time.'
'It's normal. Big hotels are slow.' Pema kept scrolling the chat, reading the agent's last message twice.
'Which hotel, actually? You never said the name.'
'They'll tell me at the offer signing.' She laughed, too quickly. 'Why are you interrogating me?'
'I'm not. Amma was asking, that's all. She's already told half the colony you're going to Dubai.'
Pema's thumb stopped. The agent's profile photo had changed since morning. 'Tell Amma not to tell people yet.'
'Pema, is something off?'
'No.' She stood and carried her tea to the balcony. 'It's fine. It has to be.'

qa.q: How many times has the visa date changed, according to Varun?
qa.a: According to Varun, this is the third time the date has changed.

qa.q: What does Pema's 'It's fine. It has to be.' reveal?
qa.a: It shows Pema is anxious and torn: part of her already suspects something is wrong, but she badly wants the job to be real, especially now that Amma has told the colony.

qa.q: What could open a way out for Pema at this stage?
qa.a: If Varun keeps his tone calm and offers to check the agent and hotel together through official sources, Pema might find it easier to admit the doubt without losing face.

qa.q: What is Varun experiencing as Pema walks off to the balcony?
qa.a: He is likely worried and confused; he noticed the shifting dates and the missing hotel name, but got shut out when he asked.

grounding: It shows a victim noticing inconsistencies yet clinging to hope, with the fear of her family's and neighbours' reaction making it hard to speak.

passage:
Looking back at those two weeks, I knew. I just didn't let myself finish the thought.
The trading dashboard showed my 40,000 had grown to 1.2 lakh, but every withdrawal request came back 'pending review'. The support chat used three different names in one evening. Once, the 'senior analyst' called me Arif.
I noticed all of it. And each time I'd open the dashboard again, look at the green number and feel calmer.
Part of that money was from Abbu, for my course fees. I rehearsed telling him and could only picture his silence at the dinner table, and my uncles hearing about it at Eid.
Karthik, from my team, asked once why I kept checking my phone in meetings. 'Market stuff,' I said, and changed the subject.
Weeks later he told me, 'Asif, you looked grey for a fortnight.'

qa.q: What name did the 'senior analyst' once call Asif by mistake?
qa.a: The senior analyst once called Asif 'Arif'.

qa.q: Why did Asif keep opening the dashboard despite the warning signs?
qa.a: Looking at the green number made Asif feel calmer and kept the hope alive, which was easier than facing the fear of telling Abbu.

qa.q: What could have helped Asif break out of the denial sooner?
qa.a: Writing the warning signs down and telling one calm person, like Karthik, could have made the doubt harder to push aside and lowered the shame of speaking.

qa.q: How might Karthik have seen Asif during those two weeks?
qa.a: Karthik saw a colleague who looked grey and kept checking the phone in meetings, and probably sensed trouble but was brushed off with 'market stuff'.

grounding: It shows someone who sees the inconsistencies but hopes they mean nothing, held back from telling anyone by fear of a parent's reaction and family shame.

passage:
In the small town of Dhrangadhra, Samir had been paying "release charges" for three months on an insurance policy that a caller said had matured. Each time, the officer promised the cheque for next week.
This week there were new cracks. The "head office" letter spelled the company's name wrong. The officer's number changed twice. When Samir asked for the branch address, the man laughed and said, "Trust me, Samir bhai."
At night Samir lay awake beside his wife, Neelam, doing sums in his head. Part of him knew. Part of him kept hoping the cheque would arrive and he'd never have to explain the savings missing from the tin they had been filling for her brother's wedding gift.
When Neelam asked why he had stopped eating, he said, "The shop is slow." He couldn't bear her face, or her father's, if they learned he'd been fooled.

qa.q: What did the head office letter get wrong?
qa.a: It spelled the company's name wrong.

qa.q: Why is Samir afraid to tell Neelam?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and afraid of losing face with Neelam and her father, so he clings to hope instead.

qa.q: What could help Samir break the denial?
qa.a: Checking the insurer's official number himself, telling Neelam the truth, and reporting to the bank and cyber-crime helpline.

qa.q: What might Neelam be noticing in Samir?
qa.a: Neelam notices his sleeplessness and lost appetite and feels worried, sensing it is more than a slow shop.

grounding: A young man sees growing inconsistencies in a fake insurance payout but hopes he is wrong, afraid of shame before his wife's family.

passage:
Gabriel had paid the recruitment agency in Manila four instalments for a warehouse job in Canada: visa processing, medicals, training, a "priority slot". His mother had pawned her earrings for the third payment.
This week Tuan, his co-worker at the call centre, mentioned that the agency's office address on its website was a car park. Gabriel laughed too loudly. "They probably moved."
But that night he looked it up himself. The street view showed a car park. The agency's licence number didn't appear on the government list. His stomach dropped, and then, almost at once, a voice in him said: maybe it's an old listing. Maybe it's fine.
He didn't tell his mother. How could he? For months she had been telling the neighbours her son was going to Canada. He lay awake till four, phone on his chest, rereading the agency's cheerful messages.

qa.q: What did the street view show at the agency's address?
qa.a: A car park.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling when the inner voice said 'maybe it's fine'?
qa.a: He felt a sick fear and a desperate hope, not wanting to face the shame of telling his mother.

qa.q: What small step could Gabriel take the next morning?
qa.a: Tell Tuan what he found, check the licence with the official government office, and stop any further payment.

qa.q: What might Gabriel's mother feel if she learned the truth?
qa.a: She might feel shocked and grieved about the earrings, but also relieved her son told her before losing more.

grounding: A young man finds clear signs that a job agency is fake but hopes it is not, too ashamed to tell his mother.

passage: In the bank's staff canteen, Payal pushed her dal around and kept checking her phone. The man she had been messaging for four months, a doctor working abroad, he said, had asked again for money to clear his "stuck" salary. Last week his camera was broken. Yesterday he wrote that he was in London; today the time on his message said it was 3 am there, yet he was "just finishing lunch." Payal noticed. She told herself time zones were confusing. Her colleague Sudha sat down. "You've been quiet all week. Everything okay at home?" Payal smiled too quickly. "All fine. Just tired." She could not imagine saying it aloud: that she, who processed loans all day, might have been fooled. Her mother would never let it go. Her cousins would hear by evening. She turned the phone face down and hoped, very hard, that she was wrong.

qa.q: Where did the man say he was yesterday?
qa.a: Yesterday he wrote that he was in London.

qa.q: Why does Payal smile too quickly when Sudha asks if everything is okay?
qa.a: Payal is afraid and ashamed, hoping the doubts are wrong because telling anyone would mean facing her mother, her cousins and her own sense of being fooled.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Payal right now?
qa.a: Payal could take up Sudha's opening and tell her what she has noticed, then check the man's story and send nothing more until she has spoken to someone she trusts.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel after Payal says all fine?
qa.a: Sudha may feel uneasy and unconvinced, having noticed a week of quiet, and may wonder how to ask again without pushing.

grounding: Shows a victim noticing inconsistencies but hoping they are wrong, with fear of shame and family reaction keeping her silent.
